title: Your First GPR Surrogate
description: Walk through the full upload → clean → train → predict workflow on a smooth 2-input quadratic function. By the end you will have a trained GPR and understand what each step does.

steps.instruction: The dataset has been loaded. Review the 10-row preview. Notice the column names — x1 and x2 are your two input variables, y is the output you want to predict.
Open the scatter matrix (Step 3). Look at the x1 vs y and x2 vs y plots.

quiz.question: What kind of relationship does the x1 vs y scatter suggest?
options: Linear (straight line)
Quadratic (curved)
No relationship
Exponential
quiz.explanation: The curved shape in the scatter indicates a nonlinear (quadratic) relationship. A linear model would underfit this data, making GPR a better choice here.

steps.instruction: Open Step 4 — Clean. The dataset is already clean (no nulls, no outliers). You can skip to the next step. In real projects this step is where you handle missing values and outliers.
Open Step 6 — Assign. Set x1 and x2 as Input columns and y as the Output column.

quiz.question: Why must you designate columns before training?
options: To rename the columns
So the model knows which variables are predictors and which is the target
To remove unused columns from memory
It is not required — the model detects inputs automatically
quiz.explanation: The surrogate learns a function from inputs to outputs. Without telling the tool which columns play which role, it cannot construct the training matrix X and target vector y.

steps.instruction: Open Step 7 — Normalize. Select Min-Max and click Apply. Min-Max is chosen here because x1 and x2 have known, bounded ranges — it scales every input to [0, 1] so neither variable overshadows the other just because it has larger numbers. Z-Score (the alternative) is better suited when data may have outliers or an unbounded range. Once you see the green success notification, you can move on.

quiz.question: What happens if you skip normalization before training?
options: Nothing — the model handles it automatically
Inputs with larger numeric ranges will have more influence on the model than inputs with smaller ranges, even if they are less important
The model will throw an error
Training will be faster
quiz.explanation: The model measures how similar two data points are by looking at the distance between them. If x1 goes from 0 to 1000 and x2 goes from 0 to 1, a small step in x1 looks much bigger than a large step in x2 — even if x2 matters more. Scaling both to the same range removes that bias.

steps.instruction: Open Step 8 — Filter Inputs. This panel checks for redundant or uninformative inputs using correlation and sensitivity analysis. For this clean 2-input dataset there is nothing to remove — skip it and move on. We will use this panel properly in Exercise 6.

Open Step 9 — Model. Select GPR as the model type. Leave the test split at 0.2 and CV folds at 5. GPR (Gaussian Process Regression) is a model that learns not just a prediction, but also how confident it is — useful when your data is limited and you need to know where the model might be wrong.

quiz.question: Why is GPR a good choice for this small, smooth 2-input dataset?
options: GPR is the fastest model to train
GPR is designed for small datasets and gives a confidence estimate alongside every prediction
GPR requires the fewest settings to configure
GPR is the only model that works with 2 inputs
quiz.explanation: GPR works well when you have a limited number of experiments and a smooth response. It learns from patterns between nearby data points and tells you how certain it is about each prediction — a useful safety check when making engineering decisions based on the surrogate.

steps.instruction: Train the model (Step 9). After training, review the R² score and the parity plot. A well-fit model should have R² > 0.90 on this clean dataset. Overfitting means the model memorised the training data but fails on new data (high CV R², low test R²). Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the pattern (low R² on both).

quiz.question: On the parity plot, what does it mean if points cluster tightly along the diagonal?
options: The model has overfit the training data
Predicted values closely match true values — the model is accurate
The model is underfitting
The test split was too small
quiz.explanation: The parity plot compares predicted vs actual values on the held-out test set — rows the model never saw during training. Points on the diagonal mean prediction = truth. Points scattered far from it indicate error. A curve or systematic bend means the model is missing a pattern in the data (underfitting).

steps.instruction: Open Step 11 — Predict. Set x1 = 5.0, x2 = -2.0. Notice the red extrapolation warning that appears below the x1 field — x1 = 5.0 is well outside the training range. The model will still return a prediction, but it is unreliable here: there is no training data nearby to anchor it.

quiz.question: What does an extrapolation warning mean?
options: The model crashed
Your input value is outside the range the model was trained on — treat the prediction with caution
The prediction is wrong
You need to retrain the model
quiz.explanation: Surrogates interpolate within the training data envelope. When you request a prediction outside that envelope, the model is extrapolating — it has no data to support the prediction there, so uncertainty is higher.
